title: Trump tried to curb clean energy. It’s booming anyway.
gist: US clean energy additions are set to hit a record 45 GW in 2026 — about 25 percent above the 2024 record — because AI data center power demand, a July 4 tax-credit start-construction deadline, and Iran-war-driven fuel prices overwhelmed the Trump administration's attempts to block solar and wind. Courts and pragmatic permitting decisions have blunted the policy attack, while expiring IRA subsidies are expected to push electricity prices up 40–120 percent, handing developers unusually strong economics.

themes.theme: Record capacity additions despite policy hostility

insights.claim: US clean energy additions will rise by a record 45 gigawatts in 2026 according to S&P Global Energy — roughly 25 percent above the record set in 2024, and equivalent to the average electricity demand of Turkey.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Volume growth, not policy support, is the driver — renewables developers and equipment suppliers can beat consensus estimates built on a policy-driven slowdown.
insights.quote: Clean energy additions will rise by a record 45 gigawatts this year, according to S&P Global Energy—equivalent to the average electricity demand of Turkey.
insights.locator: Clean energy additions will rise by

insights.claim: S&P projects new US solar capacity to jump by nearly a third in 2026 and new wind capacity by almost 50 percent, with solar setting another record in 2027 while wind falls back before recovering.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The wind pipeline has a visible 2027 air pocket while solar keeps compounding — favor solar-and-storage exposure over pure-play wind for the 2027 book.
insights.quote: S&P said new solar and wind capacity will jump in 2026 by nearly a third and almost 50 percent respectively.
insights.locator: S&P said new solar and wind capacity

insights.claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's July 4 start-construction deadline pulled forward a wave of solar and wind builds, since developers who broke ground by that date have until 2030 to finish and still capture the tax credits.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Much of the current boom is a pulled-forward safe-harbor backlog with a hard 2030 completion wall — model a demand cliff after that pipeline is worked off.
insights.quote: prompted developers to hurry and begin construction
insights.locator: But under the terms of the OBBBA

themes.theme: Demand shock from data centers and electrification

insights.claim: US power consumption is expected to grow 39 percent by 2035 according to consultancy ICF, driven by data centers and the electrification of household appliances and transport, after more than a decade of flat demand.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: A decade-long flat-demand regime has broken; utilities, grid equipment, and independent power producers are repricing against a structurally different load curve.
insights.quote: US power consumption is expected to grow 39 percent by 2035, according to consultancy ICF
insights.locator: US power consumption is expected to grow

insights.claim: Data center operators need power on such short notice that speed-to-grid, not ideology, is deciding generation mix — new solar and wind sites have a lead time of under two years versus at least three years for gas projects, according to RMI.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Time-to-power is the binding constraint in the AI buildout; assets that can be energized fastest capture the scarcity premium regardless of federal preference.
insights.quote: Data centers need power, and they need it basically yesterday.
insights.locator: Candidly, it’s a good time to be a developer

insights.claim: An energy infrastructure investor argues the administration reversed course in practice because power demand makes renewables non-optional, not because of any change in stated policy.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Political headline risk overstates real regulatory risk to renewables cash flows — a gap that creates mispricing in developer equities.
insights.quote: There was a campaign promise to go against renewables, but at the same time they’re realizing that you can’t do without it

insights.claim: Lazard puts solar and wind breakeven at as little as $38 and $37 per megawatt-hour respectively versus at least $48/MWh for gas, though those figures exclude system upgrade costs and the batteries needed to smooth intermittency.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The headline cost gap is real but understated on the renewables side — the true trade is in storage and transmission upgrades that the LCOE comparison omits.
insights.quote: Producers can break even by selling solar and wind power for as little as $38 and $37 per megawatt-hour, respectively, compared to at least $48 per megawatt-hour for gas
insights.locator: Producers can break even by selling

insights.claim: Electricity prices are expected to rise 40 to 120 percent once the Inflation Reduction Act subsidies expire, which mechanically expands margins for renewable power developers selling into those markets.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Subsidy removal is a revenue tailwind, not a headwind, for developers with assets already built — but a consumer-cost political flashpoint to watch.
insights.quote: electricity prices are expected to rise 40 to 120 percent once Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act subsidies expire
insights.locator: Renewable power developers also stand to profit

themes.theme: Consumer-side demand from war and extreme weather

insights.claim: Consumer investment in residential solar panels, batteries, and zero-emission vehicles led US clean energy spending in Q2 2026, rising 45 percent from the prior quarter and 21 percent year over year, according to Rhodium Group.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The consumer segment is accelerating faster than utility-scale — residential solar and storage installers may be underpriced relative to their sequential growth.
insights.quote: increasing 45 percent from the previous quarter and 21 percent from the same period in 2025
insights.locator: Consumer investment in residential solar panels

insights.claim: Hurricane risk and Iran-war fuel prices are pulling consumers into home batteries and electrified vehicles for resilience and cost reasons rather than climate motives, per Rhodium's energy and climate practice.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Demand drivers are grid reliability and fuel cost, so this segment is insulated from a political backlash against 'green' framing.
insights.quote: People in Florida are installing a lot of home batteries to ensure their house still has power in a hurricane

themes.theme: Litigation and permitting as the real gating factor

insights.claim: Courts have blocked all five of the administration's attempts to halt construction at wind projects off the US East Coast, and an Oregon district judge ordered the Pentagon to stop blocking onshore wind development.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The judicial track record is a five-for-five backstop against executive interference — a concrete reason to discount project-cancellation risk in offshore wind.
insights.quote: The courts have blocked all five of the administration’s attempts to halt construction at wind projects off the US’s East Coast.
insights.locator: US courts have slowed Trump’s war on green energy

insights.claim: Developers are winning individual permits by lobbying the administration directly through people with ties to it, and by arguing that their projects will not displace fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Political access is now a differentiating asset for developers — permitting outcomes will diverge sharply by sponsor, not by project quality.
insights.locator: Developers are having some success lobbying

insights.claim: The administration killed Esmeralda 7 in Nevada, which would have been the largest single solar project in the US, and has interfered with routine approvals for more than 150 onshore wind projects.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Headline project cancellations are real and concentrated — single-project exposure carries policy risk even as the aggregate build accelerates.
insights.quote: The Trump administration broke up Esmeralda 7 in Nevada. It would have been the largest single solar project in the US.
insights.locator: The Trump administration broke up Esmeralda 7

insights.claim: Permitting officials are proving pragmatic on land with no competing economic use, according to a clean energy CEO citing the corridor between Reno, Tucson, and Barstow as ideal for solar-plus-storage.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Geography is a permitting hedge: Southwest desert solar-plus-storage faces the least approval friction of any renewable category.
insights.quote: There’s a lot of land between Reno, Tucson, and Barstow, where there’s no better use than solar-plus-storage.
insights.locator: What we found on the permit side
